front: What is a wave? Give the pond-pebble picture.
back: A disturbance generated at one point (a pebble dropped) travels to other points as a pattern — circular ripples expand while cork pieces merely bob up and down, never moving radially outward. So a wave is a pattern moving WITHOUT the physical flow/transfer of matter as a whole: energy and the disturbance pattern travel, while the medium oscillates about fixed positions. Waves carry energy and information — all communication relies on wave transmission.

front: Distinguish mechanical, electromagnetic and matter waves.
back: Mechanical waves (string, water, sound, seismic) need a medium — its constituent oscillations plus elastic properties generate them; they cannot pass through vacuum. Electromagnetic waves need no medium; in vacuum all travel at c = 299,792,458 m s⁻¹ (14.1). Matter waves are associated with electrons/protons/atoms (quantum); used in electron microscopes. This chapter treats mechanical waves only.

front: Define transverse and longitudinal waves.
back: Transverse: constituents oscillate PERPENDICULAR to the direction of propagation (an up-down jerk on a string sends the pulse along the string). Longitudinal: constituents oscillate ALONG the direction of propagation (a piston in an air-filled pipe generates pulses of condensations and rarefactions; a continuous sinusoidal push-pull gives a sinusoidal longitudinal wave). A wave can be viewed either as a shape in space at a fixed instant or as an element's SHM in time at a fixed location.

front: Which media support transverse vs longitudinal waves — and why air only has sound?
back: Transverse waves need shearing stress, so only media that sustain shear — SOLIDS — support them; fluids do not. Longitudinal waves need bulk (compressive) strain, so ALL elastic media (solids, liquids, gases) support them. Steel supports both; air supports only longitudinal. Water surface waves (capillary ~cm by surface tension; gravity, metres–hundreds of m, by gravity) involve a combination of up-down and back-forth particle motion. Transverse and longitudinal waves travel with different speeds in the same medium.

front: Write the phase-velocity form of a sinusoidal wave and explain the −/+ signs.
back: y(x,t) = a sin(kx − ωt + φ) (14.2) travels along +x: keeping the phase constant as t grows requires x to increase. y = a sin(kx + ωt + φ) (14.4) travels along −x. Equivalently y = A sin(kx − ωt) + B cos(kx − ωt) (14.3) with a = √(A² + B²) and tan φ = B/A. Fix t → sine shape in space; fix x → SHM in time.

front: Define amplitude, phase and initial phase of a progressive wave.
back: Amplitude a: the positive magnitude of maximum displacement; y oscillates between +a and −a. Phase (kx − ωt + φ): determines the displacement at any x and t once a is known. Initial phase angle φ: the phase at x = 0 and t = 0. By choosing the origin of space and time suitably one may take φ = 0 without loss of generality.

front: Define wavelength λ and angular wave number k.
back: λ is the minimum distance between two points of the same phase — e.g. consecutive crests or troughs. With φ = 0 at t = 0, y = a sin kx (14.5); sine repeats after a phase change of 2π, so kλ = 2π and λ = 2π/k (14.6). k is the angular wave number (propagation constant), SI unit rad m⁻¹ (radians dropped → reads as m⁻¹), equal to 2π times the number of complete waves per unit length.

front: Define period, frequency and angular frequency for a wave.
back: Monitoring the element at x = 0, y(0,t) = −a sin ωt: period T is the time for one full oscillation; since ωT = 2π, ω = 2π/T (14.7) in rad s⁻¹. Frequency ν = 1/T = ω/2π (14.8) in Hz. The same equation describes a longitudinal wave with a displacement along the propagation direction: s(x,t) = a sin(kx − ωt + φ) (14.9).

front: How is the speed of a travelling wave derived from the phase?
back: Follow a point of constant phase: kx − ωt = constant (14.10). Letting t → t + Δt with the point moving to x + Δx to keep the phase, kΔx − ωΔt = 0, so v = dx/dt = ω/k (14.11). Since ω = 2πν and k = 2π/λ this gives v = λν = λ/T (14.12): in one period the pattern advances one wavelength. The speed is set by the medium's inertial (μ or ρ) and elastic (moduli) properties — NOT by the source; the source frequency then fixes λ via λ = v/ν.

front: Speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string.
back: Restoring force = tension T; inertial property = linear mass density μ = m/L. Dimensionally T/μ has units (MLT⁻²)/(ML⁻¹) = L²T⁻², giving v = √(T/μ) (14.14). The speed depends ONLY on the medium (T, μ), not on λ or ν; with a source of frequency ν, λ = v/ν (14.15). Example: a 0.72 m, 5.0 × 10⁻³ kg wire under 60 N has μ = 6.9 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹ and v = √(60/6.9×10⁻³) ≈ 93 m s⁻¹.

front: Speed of longitudinal (sound) waves in fluids and solids.
back: Elastic property = bulk modulus B = −ΔP/(ΔV/V) (14.16) in Pa; inertial property = ρ. Since B/ρ has dimensions L²T⁻², v = √(B/ρ) (14.19) for longitudinal waves in a fluid. For a long solid bar (longitudinal strain only) use Young's modulus: v = √(Y/ρ) (14.20). Liquids/solids have higher sound speeds than gases because their much larger bulk modulus outweighs their higher density.

front: Newton vs Laplace for the speed of sound in a gas.
back: In an ideal gas PV = Nk_BT (14.21). Newton assumed isothermal changes, B = P, giving v = √(P/ρ) (14.22) — about 280 m s⁻¹ at STP (air: molar mass 29.0 × 10⁻³ kg, molar volume 22.4 L ⇒ ρ = 1.29 kg m⁻³), ~15% below the measured 331 m s⁻¹. Laplace noted pressure changes are too fast for heat flow — adiabatic, PV^γ = constant, so B = γP and v = √(γP/ρ) (14.24). For air γ = 7/5 this gives 331.3 m s⁻¹, matching measurement.

front: State the superposition principle and the interference of two equal waves.
back: y(x,t) = y₁(x,t) + y₂(x,t) (14.25); in general y = Σ fᵢ(x − vt) (14.26). For two equal-amplitude waves with the same ω and k but a phase difference φ, the resultant is y = 2a cos(φ/2) sin(kx − ωt + φ/2) (14.31) with amplitude A(φ) = 2a cos(φ/2) (14.32). φ = 0 (in phase): A = 2a, CONSTRUCTIVE (14.33). φ = π (out of phase): y = 0 everywhere, DESTRUCTIVE (14.34). The two original pulses retain their identity after crossing.

front: Compare reflection at a rigid vs an open boundary.
back: Rigid boundary (string fixed at a wall): reflected pulse has the same shape but a phase change of π, y_r = −a sin(kx − ωt) (14.35); the boundary displacement is y + y_r = 0 at all times (a node) — as in an echo. Non-rigid/open boundary (string on a freely moving ring, open end of a pipe): reflection with NO phase change, y_r = a sin(kx − ωt) (14.36); the displacement reaches twice the amplitude, 2a, at the boundary. At an interface between media part is reflected and part transmitted.

front: How do standing waves form, and where are the nodes and antinodes?
back: Two equal waves travelling in opposite directions superpose: y₁ = a sin(kx − ωt), y₂ = a sin(kx + ωt) give y = 2a sin kx cos ωt (14.37). x and t separate: every element oscillates with the same ω and phase but amplitude 2a|sin kx|. Nodes (amplitude 0) at x = nλ/2 (14.38), n = 0,1,2,…; antinodes (|sin kx| = 1) at x = (n + ½)λ/2 (14.39); node–node or antinode–antinode spacing = λ/2. Nodes are fixed in time — energy is not transported along, hence 'standing'.

front: Normal modes of a string fixed at both ends.
back: Both ends are nodes and the length L must fit n half-wavelengths: L = nλ/2 (14.41), so λ = 2L/n and ν = nv/2L (14.42), n = 1,2,3,… The n = 1 mode is the fundamental/first harmonic ν₁ = v/2L; n = 2, 3, … are the second, third, … harmonics. A general vibration is a superposition of modes; where/how the string is plucked or bowed decides which modes dominate (sitar, violin). Forced oscillation at a natural frequency produces resonance.

front: Harmonics of a pipe closed at one end vs open at both ends.
back: Closed at one end (node) with antinode at the other: L = (n + ½)λ/2 (14.43) so ν = (2n + 1)v/4L (14.44), n = 0,1,2,… — fundamental v/4L and ONLY odd harmonics v/4L, 3v/4L, 5v/4L. Open at both ends (antinodes at both ends): all harmonics ν = nv/2L. A circular membrane (tabla) is a 2-D version of the same standing-wave physics — forced resonance occurs when the driving frequency matches a natural frequency.

front: Work the 30 cm pipe problem (Example 14.5) with v = 330 m s⁻¹.
back: Open at both ends: fundamental ν₁ = v/2L = 330/0.6 = 550 Hz, nth mode = 550n Hz — 1.1 kHz = 2 × 550 Hz is the SECOND harmonic, so the pipe resonates at 1.1 kHz. Closed at one end: fundamental = v/4L = 330/1.2 = 275 Hz; 1100/275 = 4 would force the 4th harmonic, but a closed pipe supports only odd harmonics — hence NO resonance at 1.1 kHz.

front: What are beats and how do they arise?
back: Two harmonic waves of close but unequal frequencies superpose. At one location with equal amplitudes (phase π/2 each), s₁ = a cos ω₁t and s₂ = a cos ω₂t give s = 2a cos[(ω₁−ω₂)t/2] cos[(ω₁+ω₂)t/2] (14.46–14.47): the wave oscillates at the average frequency while its amplitude waxes/wanes at the beat frequency ν_b = ν₁ − ν₂ (14.48). Example: 11 Hz and 9 Hz give 2 beats per second. Musicians tune instruments by minimizing the beats they hear.

front: Solve the sitar tuning puzzle (Example 14.6).
back: String A sounds 427 Hz and produces 5 beats/s with B: ν_B = 427 ± 5 = 422 or 432 Hz. Increasing B's tension RAISES ν_B; the beats fall to 3 Hz. If ν_B were above ν_A, raising it would INCREASE the beats — contradiction — so ν_B < ν_A and ν_B = 427 − 5 = 422 Hz.

front: Why do sound waves travel fastest in solids and slowest in gases?
back: v = √(B/ρ): the bulk modulus of solids/liquids is so much larger than that of gases that despite their higher density the ratio B/ρ is larger. Sound speeds are ~331 m s⁻¹ (air), ~1486 m s⁻¹ (water) and ~5060 m s⁻¹ (steel). The same idea sets wave speeds in any medium: the elastic (restoring) property over the inertial property.

front: Sum up the Musical Pillars of the Nellaiappar temple.
back: In this 7th-century Pandyan-era temple (Tamil Nadu), pillars carved from a single rock produce the swaras Sa, Re, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni, Sa when tapped. Three categories of pillars: Shruti (basic notes/swaras), Gana Thoongal (ragas) and Laya Thoongal (taal/beats); some combine Shruti with Laya. The note depends on the stone's elasticity, density and shape — a real-world standing-wave/forced-vibration phenomenon. Similar pillars exist at Hampi, Kanyakumari and Thiruvananthapuram.
